lead: Every control system tries to hold one physical quantity at a value you choose. A room heater, a water tank, a car's speed — each has a target and a measured result. Open-loop control acts on the target alone and never looks at the result. Closed-loop control measures the result, compares it with the target, and uses the difference to correct itself. That one idea, feedback, separates the two families. It explains why a toaster burns toast but a fridge does not freeze the milk, and how a drone holds its height in wind.
prereq: You need: only school algebra and the idea of a function of time; Laplace and transfer functions start in 1.3.

sections.h3: The parts of a control system

blocks.text: A control system forces one physical quantity to follow a target. That quantity is the output, written y(t). The target is the reference or set point, written r(t). Both change with time t, measured in seconds.

items: Plant — the physical process being controlled: the room, the motor, the water tank.
Controller — the device that decides what to do, from the reference and the error.
Actuator — the part that turns the decision into real action: heater coil, motor drive, valve.
Sensor — the measuring element that converts the output into a signal the controller can compare: thermometer, tachometer, float switch.

blocks.text: The error is the gap between target and result. With negative feedback it is the subtraction at the summing junction.

blocks.where: e(t) is the error in the same unit as the reference (for example °C); r(t) is the reference or set point; y(t) is the measured output. The minus sign is the whole point — the controller pushes in the direction that shrinks the gap.

blocks.text: A disturbance is any unwanted input that pushes the output away from the target: a window opened in a heated room, a load torque on a motor, cold water entering a tank.
The path from reference to output is the forward path. The path that carries the measured output back to the comparison is the feedback path.

Open-loop control drives the plant from the reference alone. There is no sensor, no feedback path, no comparison. The controller is really a schedule: it knows what to do, not what happened. The block order is reference → controller → actuator → plant → output.

items: A toaster runs a timer; it has no colour sensor.
A washing machine runs a fixed wash cycle at fixed agitator speed.
A traffic light steps through a fixed timing sequence.
A stepper motor is moved a fixed number of steps with no encoder.
A room heater is switched on for 20 min at 0.5 °C/min from 20 °C, so the room reaches 30 °C — small room, large room, or open window alike.

blocks.text: Advantages: no sensor to buy or calibrate, so it is cheap and simple. The output cannot oscillate because of feedback, since there is no feedback; stability depends only on the forward path.

Disadvantages: a disturbance runs its full course uncorrected. Component drift — an ageing heater, a worn pump — shifts the output with nothing to pull it back. Accuracy depends entirely on calibration done beforehand, and a wrong setting gives a wrong result silently.
Closed-loop control measures the output and uses the error. One cycle of operation:

items: The sensor measures the output y(t).
At the summing junction the reference is compared with the measurement: e(t) = r(t) − y(t).
The controller converts e(t) into an actuator signal.
The actuator drives the plant, so the output moves.
One cycle later the sensor measures again. The loop repeats.

blocks.text: When the sensor gain is exactly 1, so that the fed-back signal is in the same units as the reference, the loop is called unity negative feedback. A sensor with gain H(s) is handled by the feedback rule in 1.8.

The simplest closed-loop action is two-position (on-off) control: the actuator is either fully on or fully off. The output then swings in a small band around the target — the fridge compressor, the electric iron, the water heater in a Chennai flat. Proportional, PI and PID actions come in Unit 5.
Advantages: disturbances are corrected, parameter drift is corrected, and the final output can be far more accurate than the individual components.
Disadvantages: the sensor costs money and needs calibration, sensor noise enters the loop, and too much loop gain causes oscillation or instability (Unit 3). More parts mean more failure points.
Labels: one reference and one output is SISO, single-input single-output. Several inputs and outputs is MIMO. The room heater is SISO; a car with throttle and steering is MIMO.

Physiological example: the body holds core temperature near 37 °C. Sensors in the skin and hypothalamus measure, the hypothalamus acts as controller, and sweating and shivering are the actuators. Fever is a disturbance that shifts the set point itself.

figure.caption: The sensor closes the loop: room temperature T is subtracted at the summing junction from the 25 °C target, and the error e drives the controller and heater. Compare an open-loop heater, where nothing is fed back and the room simply heats for as long as the timer runs.

spec.title: Closed-loop room heater
spec.aria: A closed-loop room heater: the sensor feeds room temperature back to the summing junction against the target of 25 °C.

examples.question: A room heater raises the room temperature at 0.5 °C/min while it is on, and the room cools negligibly. The room starts at 20 °C. (a) Open-loop: the heater is switched on for 20 min. Find the final temperature. (b) Closed-loop: a thermostat with target 25 °C checks the sensor once every minute and keeps the heater on while T < 25 °C. Find the heater on-time and the final temperature.
steps: Open-loop temperature rise = rate × time = 0.5 °C/min × 20 min = 10 °C.
Open-loop final temperature = 20 °C + 10 °C = 30 °C. Heater on-time = 20 min.
Minute check: after 1 min T = 20.5 °C < 25 °C, heater stays on; after 9 min T = 24.5 °C < 25 °C, still on; after 10 min T = 25.0 °C, which is not less than 25 °C, so the heater switches off.
Closed-loop final temperature = 25 °C, heater on-time = 10 min. The open-loop heater overshoots the target by 5 °C and stays there.
examples.answer: Open-loop: final temperature 30 °C with 20 min on-time. Closed-loop: final temperature 25 °C with 10 min on-time.
examples.check:
rate = 0.5
start = 20.0
T_open = start + rate * 20.0
print(T_open)

target = 25.0
T = start
on_time = 0.0
while T < target:
    T = T + rate * 1.0
    on_time = on_time + 1.0
print(T)
print(on_time)

traps: A controller does not make a system closed-loop. Without a sensor and a feedback path back to the summing junction, the loop is open — a timer with a fancy display is still a timer.
Summing-junction sign: negative feedback subtracts, so e = r − y. If you add, you get positive feedback, which drives the output away from the target.
On-off (two-position) control is closed-loop but not proportional. The actuator has only two states, so a small steady oscillation around the target is normal, not a fault.
Disturbance versus reference change: a disturbance enters at the plant, a reference change is a new target. The error signal looks similar in both cases; read where the signal enters before deciding.
Sensor gain: if a thermometer outputs 10 mV per °C, the feedback path is not unity. Convert to the reference's units before subtracting, or the error carries a hidden scale factor.

quiz.q: Define plant, actuator and sensor, giving one example of each from a room heater.
quiz.a: Plant: the process controlled, here the room. Actuator: the device that acts on the plant, here the heater coil. Sensor: the measuring element that reads the output, here a thermometer.
A closed loop in which the sensor gain is exactly 1, so the fed-back signal is in the same units as the reference and the error is e(t) = r(t) − y(t).

quiz.q: Why can an open-loop system not correct a disturbance?
quiz.a: It never measures the output, so it has no information that a disturbance has occurred. The controller keeps applying the same pre-set action while the output drifts, and nothing compares the result with the target.

quiz.q: A tank holds 100 L and fills at 5 L/min. (a) Open-loop: the pump runs 12 min. Final volume? (b) Closed-loop: target 130 L, the sensor checks every 1 min, pump on while V < 130 L. Find the on-time and final volume.
quiz.a: (a) 100 + 5 × 12 = 160 L. (b) Needed rise = 30 L; on-time = 30 ÷ 5 = 6 min; the level reaches exactly 130 L, the check V < 130 fails, pump stops. Final volume 130 L, on-time 6 min.

quiz.q: A unity-feedback loop has r = 25 °C and the measured output is 22 °C. Find the error and say what its sign means.
quiz.a: e = r − y = 25 − 22 = +3 °C. Positive error means the output is below the target, so the controller drives the heater on.

quiz.q: A technician says a system must be closed-loop because it contains a microcontroller-based controller. Critique this in two lines.
quiz.a: Loop type depends on the signal path, not on the hardware. Unless a sensor measures the output and returns it to the summing junction, the controller is acting blind and the system is open-loop.

quiz.q: A heater thermostat is set at 25 °C and someone opens a window, adding continuous heat loss. Compare the open-loop and closed-loop outcomes.
quiz.a: Open-loop: the heater runs its fixed 20 min regardless, so the room ends below 30 °C by the heat lost through the window, and the error is unknown and uncorrected. Closed-loop: the measured T rises more slowly, so the thermostat keeps the heater on longer until T reaches 25 °C; the on-time grows but the final temperature stays at the target, provided the heater can beat the loss.

beyond: Not for the exam. Every thermostat, cruise-control unit and drone autopilot on the market runs a loop of this shape. In industry the same error signal feeds a PID block inside a PLC or a DCS; what changes from our heater is tuning and sampling rate, not structure. Research moves the loop into state space, where many outputs share one controller (see Unit 6), and into model predictive control, which predicts ahead instead of reacting late. Useful search terms: PID control, closed-loop block diagram, model predictive control.
